builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Multi-step SWE: Can Coding Agents Keep Building on Their Own Code Over Long Horizons?
summary: This benchmark replaces single-task coding evaluations with 69 long-horizon tasks, each a chain of 5-15 dependent steps on one codebase, testing whether agents can build on their own prior code. It costs the effort of running multi-step evaluations and integrating verifier-based scoring into your testing pipeline, but requires no additional training or hardware beyond standard inference. Long-horizon agent chains can fail through compounding errors: early design mistakes persist, and even frontier models solve only 18.5% of tasks, so production deployments need human review and cannot assume autonomous multi-step reliability.
rationale: This is an evaluation benchmark, not a technique you can adopt; it informs tool selection and risk assessment but does not directly improve your production system.
technique: Multi-step SWE benchmark for long-horizon coding agents

claims.statement: This benchmark replaces single-task coding evaluations with 69 long-horizon tasks, each a chain of 5-15 dependent steps on one codebase, testing whether agents can build on their own prior code. It costs the effort of running multi-step evaluations and integrating verifier-based scoring into your testing pipeline, but requires no additional training or hardware beyond standard inference. Long-horizon agent chains can fail through compounding errors: early design mistakes persist, and even frontier models solve only 18.5% of tasks, so production deployments need human review and cannot assume autonomous multi-step reliability.
Across nine frontier models, the strongest model reaches a solve rate of only 18.5%, and 38 of the 69 tasks are not solved by any model.
